newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo imports to help boost industry output-agency.
newsitem.headline: Yugo imports to help boost industry output-agency.

text.p: Yugoslavia's $1.084 million trade deficit in the first half of 1997 is due to imports of raw materials and semi-finished products, which will help boost production and exports, Tanjug news agency said on Tuesday.

"Better supply of these goods should enable the increase of production and exports and create conditions for the future reduction of the trade deficit," Federal Statistics Office Director Milovan Zivkovic was quoted as saying.
Yugoslav exports stood at $1.028 billion dollars, or 28.5 percent more, than the same period last year, while imports were $2.112 billion, or 27.7 percent up, on January-June 1996.
In the first half of 1997 Yugoslavia imported semi- finished goods and raw materials to the value of $1.452 billion, or 68.7 percent of the total imports.

Yugoslavia's top export goods include non-ferrous metals ($151.3 million), iron and steel ($103.6 million), fruits and vegetables ($51.2 million), tobacco ($41.7 million), plastic materials ($45.2 million), and clothing ($33.5 million).

The list of imports was headed by oil and oil derivatives ($259.5 million), textile products ($172.4 million), mineral ores ($89.5 million), fruit and vegetables ($95.6 million), paper, cardboard and cellulose ($70.6 million).

Independent economists did not expect exports to increase dramatically due to the unfavourable trade structure. They said exports have been stagnating since June 1996, while imports have slowed due to limited funds to finance them.
June exports were down by 12.5 percent on May and imports by 30.7 percent, but trade has been known to drop in the summer months even in pre-sanction years, Zivkovic said.
Overall trade in the six-month period was $3.140 billion, 85 percent of which was with European countries.
Italy was Yugoslavia's biggest export partner with $121 worth of goods, while Germany was top on the list of countries it imported from with $315 million worth of goods, Zivkovic said.
The Russian Federation, Macedonia and Bosnian Serb republic were among Yugoslavia's biggest trading partners in the six-month period.
